title: Wingspan cast-on triangle shawl
subtitle: A bottom-up DK triangle, cast on at the full wingspan and decreased to a point.
excerpt: A bottom-up triangular shawl in DK wool, cast on at the full wingspan and decreased on every right-side row until three stitches remain at the centre-back neck. Wingspan 160 cm, centre-back depth 75 cm. About 350 g of DK yarn. A good first bottom-up shawl after the top-down construction.
sourceNotes: Bottom-up triangular shawl construction appears in Weldon's Practical Knitter, 2nd series (1886), §Shawls. The long cast-on at the wingspan edge followed by paired decreases to a centre-back point is the most common Victorian shawl structure for large wool squares and triangles.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 44 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Wingspan 160 cm. Centre-back depth 75 cm. Blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: Insert the needle through the next two stitches simultaneously from left to right and knit them as one. Creates a right-leaning decrease.
Slip the next two stitches knitwise one at a time to the right needle, then insert the left needle through the front of both slipped stitches and knit them together. Creates a left-leaning decrease.

content.text: A bottom-up DK triangle, cast on at the full wingspan and decreased every RS row to a three-stitch neck point. Wingspan 160 cm, depth 75 cm.

Bottom-up construction suits a long cast-on well: the first rows are the widest, so the shawl's final wingspan is determined by the cast-on count rather than by row count. This approach is historically the more common one for large Victorian wool shawls, where the wingspan cast-on could be adjusted for different sized shawls without changing the pattern row count. The entire body is plain garter stitch; the
decreases define the two sloped edges. Budget about 350 g (770 m / 840 yards) of DK wool.

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: About 350 g (770 m / 840 yards) of DK-weight yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 80 cm or longer

content.text: 22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. The wingspan cast-on count is calculated directly from the gauge: at 22 stitches per 10 cm, the cast-on for a 160 cm wingspan is approximately 352 stitches. If your blocked gauge reads 20 stitches per 10 cm, cast on 320 stitches. If your gauge reads 24 stitches per 10 cm, cast on 384 stitches.

Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 352 stitches (for standard 22 sts / 10 cm gauge). For the long-tail tail: at 352 stitches and 4 mm needles, leave a tail of approximately (4 × 352) / 10 + 15 = 155.8 cm, so approximately 160 cm of tail. Add the full tail before making the slip knot.
Place a marker at the midpoint of the cast-on: after stitch 176. This marks the centre back spine.
RS row: k1, ssk, k to 3 sts before marker, k2tog, k1, SM, k1, ssk, k to last 3 sts, k2tog, k1. (4 sts decreased per RS row)
Continue until 3 stitches remain (approximately 87 RS decrease rows at gauge). The shawl is now a triangle with the three-stitch point at the centre back neck.

On the final row of 3 stitches, work a standard bind-off: k2tog, pass the bound stitch over, then bind off the last stitch. The 3-stitch point is the neck edge of the shawl; only three stitches bind off here so a standard bind-off causes no restriction.
After 44 RS decrease rows: 352 - (4 × 44) = 176 stitches. Each wing holds 87 stitches. The shawl is at half-depth.
After 70 RS decrease rows: 352 - 280 = 72 stitches. The shawl is near the final point. The rows are short and progress is fast.

Cast-on edge too tight to block: the long-tail cast-on was worked at standard body tension. At 352 stitches the cast-on edge must be loose enough to pin out to the full 160 cm wingspan. If the edge feels tight, the cast-on was not worked loosely enough. Try casting on over two needles held together for an automatically looser edge.
Wings not balanced at the spine: the centre marker shifted by one stitch. Remove the marker and count to the exact midpoint before replacing it.

Ssk versus k2tog not matched: both decreases are worked on the same RS row, one each side of the centre marker. If both are k2tog the slope leans the same direction on both edges and the triangle becomes a parallelogram rather than a triangle.

Soak in cool water, press out in towels. Pin the cast-on edge straight across the full 160 cm wingspan. Pin the centre-back point (the bound-off 3-stitch end) away from the cast-on edge to the stated 75 cm depth. Pin the two sloped edges straight. Leave 24 hours.
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry.

Add a lace edging by picking up along the cast-on wingspan edge and working a narrow lace strip in the opposite direction. This gives a distinctive border without adding complexity to the main knitting.
